analysis.one_liner: Appropriates about $50 billion in emergency war funding for military operations in Iraq and Afghanistan.
analysis.headline: The roughly $50 billion Iraq and Afghanistan war funding bill never left the House Appropriations Committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, introduced by Rep. Jim Cooper of Tennessee, would have appropriated roughly $50 billion in extra 2004 spending for the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Most of it pays for troops' salaries and day-to-day operations, about $4.3 billion buys weapons and equipment, and it includes money to reimburse Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations for their help. It was referred to the House Appropriations Committee and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the bill would fund pay and operations for U.S. troops deployed in Iraq and Afghanistan, including reservists and National Guard units. Defense contractors would gain about $4.3 billion in guaranteed weapons and equipment purchases, available to spend over two years. The governments of Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations would receive reimbursements of up to roughly $890 million for logistical and military support, with the Secretary of Defense deciding how much each nation gets.

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates about $13.8 billion for military personnel across the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force, covering pay and support for troops deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan [S3].

Appropriates about $30.6 billion for operations and maintenance, including over $21 billion for the Army, plus a $1.5 billion Iraq Freedom Fund and humanitarian, disaster, and civic aid programs [S3].
Provides about $4.3 billion in procurement for weapons, tracked combat vehicles, and other equipment, available for obligating through September 2006 [S3].

Includes roughly $890 million to reimburse Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations for logistical and military support to U.S. operations, plus $56.5 million for drug interdiction activities limited to Afghanistan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, through roughly $50 billion in new federal borrowing added to the deficit. The bill designates the money an emergency requirement, which lets it bypass the budget limits Congress normally applies. Foreign reimbursement payments would be documented and sized largely at the Defense Secretary's own discretion.

drawbacks.text: The roughly $50 billion would be added to the federal deficit, and designating it an 'emergency requirement' under the FY 2004 budget resolution exempts it from the budget discipline Congress normally applies to new spending [S3].

Up to about $890 million in payments to Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations would be made in amounts the Secretary of Defense decides, based on documentation he himself determines is adequate, and his determination would be 'final and conclusive' on U.S. accounting officers — leaving only quarterly reports to Congress as outside scrutiny [S3].

About $4.3 billion in procurement (weapons, tracked combat vehicles, and other equipment) would remain available for spending through September 2006, giving defense contractors multi-year guaranteed business funded by emergency borrowing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The money would keep American troops in Iraq and Afghanistan paid, equipped, and supplied, which supporters would call essential. But the costs are real: about $50 billion added to the federal deficit, designated as an "emergency" so it bypasses the budget limits Congress normally applies [S3]. The bill also contains an unusually weak oversight provision: reimbursements to Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations would be paid based on documentation the Secretary of Defense himself deems adequate, and his determination would be "final and conclusive" on U.S. accounting officers, with only quarterly reports to Appropriations committees as a check [S3]. Loose controls on billions in foreign reimbursements were a known risk in this period, and this bill would have codified them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Appropriations Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Cooper introduced H.R. 4183 in the House on April 21, 2004; it was referred to the House Committee on Appropriations the same day [S1].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill's last recorded action is the April 21, 2004 committee referral [S5].
The bill expired with the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed because this bill died: Congress funded the wars through other supplemental appropriations instead, so no industry or group gained or lost specifically from this bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one in particular; war funding passed elsewhere

for.name: Rep. Jim Cooper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the standalone war funding bill on April 21, 2004 [S1].

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill [S4].

against.name: House Committee on Appropriations
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over all spending bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 21, 2004 and took no further recorded action — no markup, no report, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only three members attached to the bill (the sponsor and two cosponsors) were all Democrats, but with such a small group and no floor action, no partisan pattern can be read from the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill directs about $4.3 billion into procurement of weapons, tracked combat vehicles, and other equipment, plus development and sealift funds — guaranteed multi-year revenue for defense companies. For ordinary people this spending arrives as deficit-funded war costs; for contractors it is steady business tied to the wars.

industries.industry: Coalition partner governments (Pakistan, Jordan, and other cooperating nations)
industries.note: The bill would reimburse cooperating nations up to about $890 million for logistical and military support, with the Secretary of Defense deciding how much each nation receives based on documentation he accepts. This is taxpayer money flowing abroad with limited independent verification, which matters to ordinary people as both a cost and an accountability question.
